#2793. JJ Redick was impressed with the Lakers’ defense after flat start vs. Kings

For the second straight game, head coach JJ Redick praised his team's defensive performance following a sluggish start. In the Los Angeles Lakers' win over the Miami Heat on Monday, Redick complimented their second-half showing, when they limited Miami to 45 points and a 95.7 defensive rating.

On Wednesday, he was pleased with how they responded after the Sacramento Kings raced out to 16 points in the opening 4.5 minutes. Ultimately, the Lakers bounced back for a comfortable 116-103 victory and moved to 7-2 on the young season.

"I think when the game started, we were a little flat. I called an early timeout. They had 16 points. They scored 87 for the last 43:27 seconds or whatever it was [after] I called that timeout," Redick said postgame. "The promising thing on that side of the ball is the effort and the intent to execute, I think, is really high. Second efforts were really good. We had a number of veer switches and peel switches and scrambles, had a number of late shot clock possessions for them, some shot clock violations. We did a lot on that end. I think the activity overall was really good, save for the first four minutes or whatever it was."

Against the Kings, Los Angeles posted a 105.1 defensive rating, per Cleaning the Glass, which marked its third-stingiest effort of the season behind an Oct. 28 win over the Los Angeles Clippers (90.9 defensive rating) and an opening night romp of the Golden State Warriors (96.5).

The Lakers' defensive anchor, Walker Kessler, is pleased with certain aspects of their play but still sees areas to refine as the year progresses, particularly in the open floor.

"We got to clean up some stuff on the defensive end," Kessler said Wednesday. "Our half-court defense, once we get set, is pretty good. Got to do better in transition as a collective."

While the Lakers allow the seventh-fewest points per 100 transition possessions (113.2), they allow the sixth-highest transition frequency (16.9%). Thus far, that inability to slow teams is really bogging them down. Despite being seventh in transition defense and eighth in half-court defense (91.3 points per 100), they're just 16th in overall defensive rating, per Cleaning the Glass.

Despite Ja Morant's absence, they'll face a stiff test in their rematch Friday against the Portland Trail Blazers, which own the league's top-ranked offense and sit top five in both half-court and transition efficiency. Tipoff is scheduled for 7 p.m. inside Crypto.com Arena.

#2788. Can the Suns fix this from within?

Not great. Some people would pick less euphemistic words, but I'm trying to be nice. I'll admit I didn't envision this happening. I never expected the Suns to be world beaters, but I also didn't expect them to be a punching bag as they stumbled out of the gate.

The most glaring deficiency with the Suns through the first six games is defense. The Suns are second to last in points per game allowed, behind only the Chicago Bulls, at 124.3 points per game. After a bleak 1-4 start, they surrendered a season-high 132 points last night when they knew this was a critical match to right the ship. The Suns are dead last in Defensive Rating, allowing 125.6 points per 100 possessions.

The Suns need to find a lineup that can get stops. That should be the main priority in practices. Switch people around and try to get something to click. Switch people around in the games if they aren't giving maximum effort. I'm fine with anybody sitting down and watching what effort looks like.

Sometimes it appears the Suns struggle with fundamentals like switching or fighting over screens. Effort, strategy, and execution. One hand needs to know what the other is doing.

Someone I went to the game with last night, who isn't a basketball aficionado, said it just seemed like Portland was scoring so fast and easily. I guess you don't have to be a basketball genius to see the Suns suck at defense right now. She said the Suns also missed a lot of threes. The Suns could have been better. They shot 10-of-36 from deep for a 27.8% clip. Maybe if another two or three of those went in when the Suns were trying to close the gap, things could have turned out a little differently.

I told her that, the way I look at it, three-point shooting is mostly something that improves with practice. It's not like defense, where if a player gives maximum effort, their performance can improve in real time. Effort doesn't affect shooting in the same way it does defense. A lot of defense is effort, and the Suns aren't meeting the standard they set last season.

I have always considered defensive rebounding as part of defense. That word in front of rebounding is the hint. A defensive rebound ends an offensive possession, and ending the opponent's possession is important. Portland snatched 16 offensive rebounds against the Suns, who are relinquishing the third-most offensive boards in the league at 14.5 per game. Boxing out might help. I hope they realize that because they are not doing it.

The Suns need to rebound by committee. Khaman Maluach is leading the team in rebounds per 36 minutes with 11.2, but other holes in his game prevent him from being a true anchor at this early stage.

Last season, Mark Williams was second on the team in rebounds per 36 minutes, and Jordan Goodwin was sixth. Goodwin was also second in defensive rating. Getting these guys back could definitely have a positive effect, but for the Suns to turn this around, they will need to ramp up effort. This isn't just a scheme issue.

Where is the continuity, chemistry, and…. joy?

The Suns have 10 players averaging over 10 minutes a game this season. Of those 10, eight were teammates on the Suns last season. Only Miles Bridges and Luke Kennard are being incorporated into whatever system the Suns are attempting to run. This year the Suns don't look like they dislike each other, but they don't have the same energy.

One possible cause of the perceived chemistry issues is that Jalen Green is being asked to play a different role, more as a distributor. Unfortunately, through six games, he is averaging just 3.3 assists, which is exactly his career average. The Suns are now 18-20 in regular-season games when Green plays. 18-24, counting the bloodbath at the hands of the Oklahoma City Thunder. The Suns might be trying to shift from Point Book to Point Green, but right now it looks like an experiment with less-than-impressive results.

Sometimes I think it might just be easier for the Suns to get a real point guard. Then other players would be freed up to exploit their strengths. This happened when Chris Paul played with Devin Booker, and they had a decent run, but that isn't this roster.

Ott needs to determine who is best equipped for this role, since there isn't a perfect fit. If it is Green, then Jalen needs to figure this out fast. The clock is ticking. If it isn't Green, then Ott needs to figure this out fast. The clock is ticking.

I may have softened a little in the midsection as I've gotten older, but the Suns' underbelly is softer than an armadillo's. The problem is the Suns don't have a protective shell. They are just kind of soft overall right now.

Maluach looks like the game is entirely too fast for him at this stage. By the time he sees where he needs to be, the play has already evolved past the point for him to get involved. Maluach has obvious talent, but his positioning needs a lot of work and… he has hands of stone. Oso Ighodaro is averaging 4.3 assists per game and has demonstrated the ability as a playmaker to find cutting teammates for easy baskets, but he lacks the size of a true big man and will be at a disadvantage almost nightly.

The Suns need to rebound as a team. Last season Mark Williams was second on the team in rebounds per 36 minutes, and Jordan Goodwin was second. Goodwin was also second in defensive rating. Getting these guys back could definitely have an effect, but for the Suns to turn this around, they will need to ramp up effort. This isn't just a scheme issue.

Can the Suns fix this from within? I don't know. The optics have not been encouraging.

There are things that we should at least hope to see.

1. Find a lineup that clicks defensively. Practice overall schemes and implement changes specific to the opponent. Players need to give maximum effort or keep the bench warm for someone who will. Maybe Jordan Goodwin's return will help, but this needs to happen immediately. This should be attainable. Since the team is essentially worst in the league they could still be "terrible", as Dillon Brooks described… and improve.

2. Figure out the rotations and how this offense actually needs to flow. The numbers here aren't as pitiful as the defensive side, but the Suns are 26th in the league in pace, averaging only 97.3 points per 100 possessions. They are slow and constantly look disjointed. I can watch a losing team play basketball, but bad, boring basketball is a big ask.

3. Get Mark Williams and Jordan Goodwin back. The Suns' injuries are exposing their weaknesses. Defense and rebounding are the biggest culprits for this start, and those are the main things those two bring to the table. Right now nobody is eating at that table. The Suns are better equipped to suffer an injury at other positions. The Green/Brooks/Booker combo should actually give good insurance with some overlapping skills. Those two wouldn't make this team 5-1 right now, but anything would help.

4. Find a way for Booker to be a better version of himself. If Booker just plays like a good player, and not an elite All-NBA type of player, this team probably won't make the playoffs. Steve Nash won MVP in Phoenix at 30, but Booker is not passing the eye test at the same age.

5. Try harder. Please make the fans think the players want to win as bad as the fans do.

6. Prayer. If any of you are religious or spiritual, it couldn't hurt.

7. Jordan Ott's honeymoon is over. Time for the part of marriage that takes a lot of work. Hopefully Ott and the players are ready to commit. Hopefully Ott is up to the challenge. He has an imperfect roster and he has to get players in their best roles to succeed…. even if he hurts someone's feelings.

If these things don't happen, it might be a long season… or potentially short for the people who can't stomach it.

#2787. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2786. LeBron Log No. 3: The King dishes, Caitlin Clark visits and closing time

LeBron Log No. 3: The King dishes, Caitlin Clark visits and closing time originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

LeBron James' latest week with the Sixers included his first 10-assist game with Philadelphia, his best performance with the team, a visit with Caitlin Clark, a crowd-wide finger wag and one jumper he would probably like back.

Some of it belonged in the box score. The rest quickly made its way around social media.

Welcome to the third edition of the LeBron Log.

Throughout the preseason, the Sixers discussed the responsibility that accompanied their desire to play faster.

They wanted to advance the ball before defenses could organize, but Nick Nurse was not interested in accepting extra turnovers as part of the tradeoff. When asked whether he could live with more mistakes if they came with better pace, his answer was simple.

Seven games into the regular season, the Sixers have not yet become one of the NBA's fastest teams. They entered Monday ranked 20th in pace.

Philadelphia has committed an NBA-low 12.7 turnovers per game. James has helped organize the offense as its leading facilitator, recording 35 assists against 11 turnovers.

He leads the Sixers in total assists despite playing only five games. Tyrese Maxey, who has appeared in all seven, is second with 31.

James provided the cleanest example Wednesday night against the Pacers. He finished with 13 points, 10 assists, five rebounds, two blocks and no turnovers during the Sixers' 114-109 comeback victory.

It was his first double-digit-assist performance with Philadelphia. According to StatMuse, James also became the oldest player in its database to record at least 10 points and 10 assists while committing no more than one turnover.

James' night was not flashy by his standards. He attempted 12 shots and finished fifth on the team in scoring. Still, he helped five Sixers reach double figures without surrendering a possession.

The Sixers signed the NBA's all-time leading scorer. Through the opening weeks of his Philadelphia career, he has been their leading passer.

James entered his first NBA Cup game with the Sixers possessing more tournament history than anyone else on the roster.

He led the Lakers to the inaugural Cup championship in 2023 and was named the event's first MVP after averaging 26.4 points, eight rebounds and seven assists during Los Angeles' unbeaten run.

Three years later, his first Cup game in red, white and blue produced his best Sixers performance yet.

James recorded 20 points, nine rebounds, eight assists, one steal and one block in Friday's 98-93 win over the Knicks. He shot 8 for 15 and saved two of his most important baskets for the final 70 seconds.

Jalen Brunson's three-pointer gave New York a 90-89 lead with 1:32 remaining. On the ensuing possession, James backed down OG Anunoby, turned toward the middle and sank a fadeaway to move the Sixers back in front.

VJ Edgecombe extended the lead with a three-pointer as the shot clock expired. After Brunson made two free throws, Maxey drove for a layup and missed. James followed the play, collected the offensive rebound and scored the putback with 11.9 seconds remaining.

The basket sealed Philadelphia's second win over the defending champions and its first of NBA Cup group play.

"Best game all around," Nurse said. "He's been good, but that was his best game for sure."

James has played more than 1,600 regular-season games, but his Philadelphia closing reel has officially begun.

The fourth-quarter baskets were not James' only memorable moments Friday.

After converting an and-one earlier in the game, James broke out his familiar shoulder-shrug celebration. Edgecombe joined him, smiling as he mirrored the move alongside his 41-year-old teammate.

The pair had already developed a personalized handshake featuring two taps to the head and a forceful shrug. This one came during the game.

James supplied another recognizable celebration in the third quarter.

Anunoby drove toward the basket with James trailing the play. James caught him near the rim and was officially credited with his fifth block of the season.

He turned toward the crowd and wagged his finger. The fans joined in.

Edgecombe later delivered the biggest shot of the game, and James met him with an embrace near the sideline. The two are separated by more than 20 years, but they have quickly developed a collection of celebrations.

"He doesn't shy away from the moment," James said of the 21-year-old. "Young kid, but he thrives in the moment."

James was not the only basketball attraction inside Gainbridge Fieldhouse on Wednesday.

Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark watched the Sixers' win from courtside and brought a small camera with her. It was the second time this year she photographed James during a game.

In March, Clark served as a credentialed photographer when James and the Lakers visited Indiana.

"The KING 👑 … Shot by ME," Clark wrote when she shared those photos.

After Wednesday's game, Clark made her way toward the visiting locker room. She briefly met Maxey before speaking with James in the hallway.

James gave Clark one of his No. 23 Sixers jerseys. The team shared photos of the exchange with a fitting caption.

Clark publicly expressed hope that James would join the Pacers before he signed with Philadelphia. Their mutual respect goes back further.

During Clark's first WNBA season in 2024, James compared the attention surrounding her professional debut to what he experienced when he entered the NBA directly from high school.

"I'm rooting for Caitlin because I've been in that seat before," James said at the time. "I've walked that road before."

James did not speak with reporters after Wednesday's game, so he was not asked about their conversation.

Maxey was asked about meeting Clark for the first time.

"That's just another person that I like to watch," he said. "She cold. She nice. Seeing her today was really cool. Sometimes you try not to fan out, but it was really cool seeing her. It's her building; she plays here too."

James and Edgecombe also produced the week's most widely shared Sixers warmup clip.

Before Wednesday's game, the two danced together near the three-point line. Edgecombe moved away while James stepped back and launched a jumper.

The clip spread quickly across social media. James still walked out of downtown Indianapolis with 10 assists, no turnovers and a victory.

James has made more field goals than anyone in NBA history. Even the career scoring leader is entitled to one warmup mulligan.

#2784. Darien Porter returns to practice ahead of Las Vegas Raiders-San Francisco 49ers Week 9 matchup

Las Vegas Raiders cornerback Darien Porter was spotted at Thursday's practice ahead of the Week 9 matchup against the San Francisco 49ers, according to ESPN's Ryan McFadden.

Previously, Porter exited last Sunday's game against the New York Jets after suffering a groin injury on the first play from scrimmage, and he missed Wednesday's practice with the same injury. The Raiders' injury report listed him as limited for Thursday's session, a step toward being able to play this weekend.

Porter has played in seven out of eight games this season, missing Week 2 against the Los Angeles Chargers with a foot injury, and has started four contests. He's been rotating with rookie Hezekiah Masses. However, the team's other rookie corner, Jermod McCoy, originally replaced Porter when Porter went down in New York. Masses and McCoy ended up splitting reps, though, with the former recording a late pass breakup to help seal Las Vegas' win. Presumably, he'd be the starter if Porter can't go or isn't healthy enough to start.

Additionally, The Athletic's Sam Warren reported that defensive tackle Thomas Booker IV wasn't seen during Thursday's practice. Booker was limited the day before with a foot injury. He's primarily played a backup/rotational role this season. If Booker is sidelined for the game, his absence against the 49ers shouldn't change much for the Raiders' defense.

The Raiders' injury report had a few other updates as well. Defensive tackle Foley Fatukasi (shoulder/elbow) and tight end Ian Thomas (ankle) went from limited during the first practice of the week to full participants in the second. Also, wide receiver Dont'e Thornton Jr. (back) wasn't on Wednesday's report but popped up on Thursday and was limited.

Meanwhile, there's also some key injury news coming out of San Francisco. General manager John Lynch told Bay Area radio station KNBR that wide receivers Mike Evans (Achilles) and Deebo Samuel (hamstring) will not be available this week (h/t NBC Bay Area's Matt Maiocco). But the 49ers are expecting to have wideouts Demarcus Robinson and KhaDarel Hodge back this week.

The 49ers also had wide receiver Christian Kirk (knee) go from limited to did not participate, while running back Christian McCaffrey (hamstring) was upgraded to limited, and offensive tackle Trent Williams (rest) was a full participant on Thursday.

#2778. 3 takeaways from Sixers’ win over Pistons: This feels like a special group

The Sixers avenged their only loss of the young season with a 112-106 win over the Pistons in Detroit Wednesday.

It was essentially a wire-to-wire win, though it did get a bit dicey at the end. Still, the Sixers' resiliency in closing out close games remains impressive. They now have the best record in the NBA at 8-1.

Though Jalen Duren remained out for the Pistons, it was another good win for the Sixers, who remain undefeated on the road. Here are some takeaways from the victory.

Jaylen Brown was a two-way monster in this one. He was on the attack early, dropping 10 points in the first quarter and 13 in the second. He scored at all three levels, going for a coast-to-coast dunk finish over Paul Reed, operating plenty in his office in the midrange and nailing a deep three at the buzzer to close the first. He was 11-of-19 from the field and 3-of-5 from deep, finishing with a game-high 30 points.

Though VJ Edgecombe was the primary defender most of the night, Cade Cunningham saw plenty of Brown as well. They held the All-Star guard to 26 points on 9-of-22 from the field. Not a perfect night, but Cunningham had to work for everything he got.

Brown was great all night, but his biggest contribution came when it mattered most. With 38 seconds left and the Sixers clinging to a 106-102 lead, Cunningham saw an opportunity in transition to fire a triple and make it a one-point game. It was a clean look … until it wasn't. Brown recovered and came away with a massive block. From there, the Sixers put the game away at the free throw line.

Sure, there are advanced analytics that can measure a guy making "winning plays," but it's a difficult thing to quantify. It just shows up on the stat sheet as a block, but it was a game-sealing play — the kind you need to see on the court, not a spreadsheet.

As of this posting, the Sixers are second in the NBA in defensive rating. While I do think the national narrative about their defense heading into the season was slightly overblown, I wasn't expecting it to be elite right out of the gate.

The obvious locks were Brown and Edgecombe. Brown has proven to be an elite on-ball defender, while Edgecombe has all the makings of one. LeBron James has seen slippage in recent years on that end, but has been mostly excellent this season. Tyrese Maxey's defensive growth has continued as he's developed from a liability to a legitimately impactful defender.

But the biggest reason the Sixers' defense has flourished is Joel Embiid. He's moving better than he has in over two years. Though he's not quite at the level of rim protection he was during his All-Defensive Team days, he's affecting more shots at the rim. He's also looked comfortable on the perimeter — hedging, blitzing and even switching onto quicker players.

And we all know rebounding has been a massive issue here in recent seasons. Under Nick Nurse, the Sixers have finished in the bottom five in defensive rebounding percentage the last three years. As of now, the Sixers are ninth in the NBA in defensive rebounding percentage (I know, I had to double-check that one myself). Ending possessions has been huge for their defense. Embiid pulled down 15 boards Wednesday. The last time he pulled down 15 or more rebounds in regulation of a regular-season game was Jan. 22, 2024, the night he dropped 70 on Victor Wembanyama and the San Antonio Spurs.

Will this keep up? A lot of that is going to depend on health, but if they continue to play defense like this, just wait until the offense catches up.

You just get a feeling about teams early on sometimes. This group at 8-1 — playing defense, making hustle plays, closing out close games, getting along and having fun — feels special. I know, most teams that LeBron plays on feel special, but there's this focus and drive that I've never seen in any Sixers team I've covered.

They're going to hit adversity. An injury or two is sure to pop up. The offense is still in the bottom third of the league. The backup center situation is murky at best.

But man, this feels like a team worth getting excited about.

#2776. Western Christian claims program's 20th IGHSAU volleyball state title

CORALVILLE − It may feel like Groundhog Day for some Iowa high school volleyball fans, as Western Christian has claimed another state title.

The No. 1-seeded Wolfpack swept No. 6 Cherokee Washington in three sets (25-20, 25-12 and 26-24) on Thursday. Nov. 5. That's Western Christian's 20th state title, tying it with Wahlert Catholic for the most Iowa state volleyball titles. They are one of four programs to have double-digit state titles alongside Wahlert Catholic, Dike-New Hartford (16) and Tripoli (11).

Morgan Kooiman, Maddyn De Jager, Josie Hall and Hadley Dekkers led the charge for the Wolfpack on Thursday. Kooiman led the team with 17 kills, while DeJager (14) and Hall (9) combined for 23 more. Dekkers set up the trio well with 38 total assists.

Western Christian and Cherokee traded blows in the first set. Cherokee led by as much as four early on, but the Wolfpack rallied to win 25-20. Kooiman had seven kills in the set, including the final two to close on a 10-4 run. Kooiman, Hall and De Jager combined for 14 of Western Christian's 15 kills in the frame. The Wolfpack started the second set with all the momentum and took an 11-1 lead following a handful of attack errors from Cherokee Washington. Western Christian never looked back on its way to a 25-12 set victory.

Cherokee Washington refused to go down without a fight, leading by as many as four points, 19-15, in the third set. It was inches away from claiming a set for itself at 24-23 to keep its championship hopes alive. However, Hall recorded a kill, followed by back-to-back kills from Kooiman to secure a 26-24 set win and Western Christian's 20th state title.

More: How Tammi Veerbeek become the winningest HS volleyball coach in Iowa

Western Christian prepared for tight moments like that all year, situations like being tied late and needing to score, or trailing in a set and needing to rally. Because of that, it was ready for a battle to the wire even in the high-pressure state finals.

"I just felt this group had a calmness, just a, 'We can do this together, we're not going to get rattled, (attitude)'" said Western Christian coach Tammi Verbeek. "They proved it."

Cherokee Washington's stellar year wraps up at 32-9, making a deep run despite their No. 6 seed. Deidra Doeden (12), Ellana Mortenson (8) and Addy Wolfswinkel (6) combined for 26 kills in their state finals effort. This was the school's third-ever state tournament appearance.

The Wolfpack end their season at 41-5, as Verbeek continues to cement her legacy as one of the greatest Iowa high school coaches ever, with 15 state titles to her name.

"Every team is special," Verbeek said. "There's never one that you value more than another one because these girls worked hard for it. They wanted it just as bad as anyone."

#2774. Carmelo and La La Anthony reach divorce settlement — nine years after breakup

Hall of Famer Carmelo Anthony and actress La La Anthony reached a settlement five years after she filed for divorce in 2021, citing irreconcilable differences, according to court documents obtained by TMZ.

The pair, who broke up in 2017 after seven years of marriage, reportedly informed the court this week of the agreement.

The terms of their settlement are confidential and a judge has yet to sign off on it.

Carmelo Anthony and La La Anthony at the Houston Cougars-Syracuse Orange game during the Players Era Basketball Championship at MGM Grand Garden Arena on November 24, 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada. Getty Images

La La, 44, and Carmelo, 42, have remained close friends and co-parent their 19-year-old son Kiyan, a sophomore guard at Syracuse.

The elder Anthony became a star in one season at Syracuse in 2002-03, leading the Orange to a national championship.

Both La La and Carmelo have not been in serious relationships since their split.

La La Anthony and Carmelo Anthony attend the "Manus x Machina: Fashion In An Age Of Technology" Costume Institute Gala at Metropolitan Museum of Art on May 2, 2016. Getty Images

During an appearance on the "Call Her Daddy" podcast in October 2022, La La said the marriage started falling apart after Carmelo was traded from the Nuggets to the Knicks in 2011.

"When we lived here [in New York] under all of that [attention], that's when things became complicated. I think that was kind of the start, now that I look back, that was kind of the start of the demise of the marriage," La La said at the time.

"It is the hardest with the scrutiny and the media and the press, just everything. It is really hard. That's not the only reason things didn't work out, but things got tough with New York … just constantly being under the spotlight and people watching every little thing."

Carmelo Anthony shoots during the first quarter of an NBA game at MSG in New York, Feb. 27, 2017. Paul J. Bereswill

#2769. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2766. Haaland has the final say as Manchester City survive Leipzig fightback

Looking to extend their unbeaten home run, RB Leipzig welcomed Manchester City to Saxony for the fourth outing of their Champions League campaign.

Meanwhile, City, still engulfed in legal trouble, arrived hoping to return to winning ways after back-to-back Premier League defeats to Aston Villa and Brighton.

It was the hosts who made the livelier start, with Antonio Nusa providing the first meaningful effort of the encounter in the 15th minute. Cutting in from the right, the Norwegian unleashed a powerful strike from the edge of the box, though Gianluigi Donnarumma remained unfazed as the ball flew straight at him.

From there, Leipzig took control, with Nusa at the heart of proceedings as Martín Demichelis' side pinned City inside their own half for the best part of 15 minutes.

Christoph Baumgartner, Brajan Gruda and David Raum all tried their luck, while City had to wait until the 36th minute for their first effort since the early stages, with Phil Foden digging out a shot from the edge of the box following a wonderful first touch.

Yet, a matter of seconds later, Manchester City took the lead completely against the run of play.

Latching onto a long ball to the left, Nico O'Reilly sent the ball back across the box, where it failed to find a teammate. Instead, it reached the unfortunate Castello Lukeba, whose momentum left him helpless as he prodded the ball beyond Maarten Vandevoordt and into his own net.

The visitors may have edged the possession statistics, but it was Leipzig who had every reason to feel hard done by as the half-time whistle sounded.

In years gone by, this would be the point where we wax lyrical about a Manchester City side who overcame a difficult start to produce one of those marvellous midweek performances that so many across the continent have fallen victim to.

Leipzig know that feeling better than most, having conceded 22 goals in seven meetings with the 2023 European champions. This time, however, the Red Bulls had other ideas.

Demichelis' side came flying out of the blocks after the restart, with Baumgartner once again lifting the crowd with an ambitious effort from distance.

The early pressure was soon rewarded, as Leipzig found themselves level less than three minutes into the second half.

Having fallen behind in such unfortunate circumstances, there was perhaps a touch of justice in the manner of their equaliser, as Ridle Baku's attempted low cross somehow found its way into the bottom corner, catching Donnarumma off his line as the Italian anticipated a delivery into the middle.

Gruda, whose late winner against PSV had already made him a Champions League hero in his debut campaign, was pulling the strings down the right, while Demichelis turned to Christopher Nkunku from the bench, a player with a hattrick to his name against City in 2022.

Yet, for all their control, Leipzig once again found themselves staring at a deficit.

City had barely threatened since the restart, but in the 58th minute, Iliman Ndiaye delivered a wonderful ball for Enzo Fernández, who powered home to restore the visitors' advantage.

For the second time, Leipzig had been punished despite looking the better side. And for the second time, they had an answer, though their first deficit had lasted just under 10 minutes of playing time. This time around, they needed only three.

Gruda combined with Ezechiel Banzuzi on the edge of the area before substitute Nkunku picked out Nusa, who drilled an emphatic finish into the net from the left side of the box.

Having tormented City's defence from the opening exchanges, the Norwegian finally had the goal his performance deserved.

Leipzig were level again at 2-2, and City, for all their experience on the European stage, were finding this particular trip to Saxony anything but straightforward.

But for all their efforts, Leipzig found themselves undone once again, as Erling Haaland slid home to restore City's lead with just over 10 minutes remaining.

The Norwegian had been unusually quiet on the night, but if there is one lesson to be learned from City's aforementioned European exploits, it is that their towering frontman can never truly be written off.

Elliot Anderson, who had tried his luck only moments earlier, powered down the right before fizzing a dangerous ball towards the back post, where Haaland slid in to guide it into a virtually empty net for his fifth in three Champions League outings this season.

Leipzig skipper Raum and City midfielder Rayan Cherki both rattled the crossbar as the chances began to flow in the final quarter of an hour, and the hosts were not out of the clash just yet.

Four minutes of additional time were signalled, and Leipzig were handed one final opportunity when substitute Allan needlessly conceded a free-kick out on the left. But despite teasing deliveries from Raum and Gruda, City stood firm, before Jeremy Doku lifted an effort over the bar at the other end.

In the end, this was hardly a vintage Manchester City performance on the European stage. For long spells, Leipzig had been the better side, and twice they had fought their way back into the contest.

Yet, as has so often been the case on the continent, City found a way to win, condemning Demichelis to his first home defeat in charge of the club.

#2759. Kon Knueppel injury cuts his season debut short after six minutes in major Hornets worry

Kon Knueppel is right back on the shelf after lasting just six minutes in his season debut.

The promising 21-year-old Hornets wing, who finished second in the NBA Rookie of the Year voting last season, missed the first eight games of the season with a left hamstring injury, and he appeared to aggravate that issue during a loss to the Nets on Wednesday night in Brooklyn, Charlotte's fifth straight defeat.

The Hornets (3-6) attributed Knueppel's exit to "soreness in his left leg" and head coach Charles Lee did not have an update after the game.

He finished with three points, all coming on free throws, and two turnovers.

Charlotte selected Knueppel No. 4 overall out of Duke in the 2025 NBA Draft, and he finished his rookie season with averages of 18.5 points, 5.3 rebounds and 3.4 assists per game while shooting 47.5 percent from the field, including an impressive 42.5 percent from 3-point range on 7.9 attempts per game.

The Hornets decided to shift course despite their strong 2025-26 campaign, sending LaMelo Ball to the Timberwolves as part of a four-team trade that saw Charlotte acquire big man Naz Reid (a former NBA Sixth Man of the Year), along with an unprotected 2033 first-round pick, three first-round pick swaps and three second-round picks.

Brooklyn Nets forward Michael Porter Jr. defends Charlotte Hornets guard Kon Knueppel during a game on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, in Brooklyn, N.Y. Corey Sipkin for the NY POST

Reid has been off to a strong start, averaging 16.9 points and 8.3 rebounds per game, but the Hornets have hit a five-game skid after starting the season 3-1.

But without Knueppel, the Hornets will have a hard time snapping their decade-long playoff drought.

#2758. Not much has worked for the Houston Texans on the ground. Here's what has: Woody Marks and run right

The Houston Texans entered the season hoping for a revamped running game after struggling on the ground in 2025. That hasn't happened.

Entering Sunday's game against the Los Angeles Chargers, the Texans rank fourth-worst in the league in yards per carry and have the second-fewest carries through eight weeks.

"I want us to move the football," coach DeMeco Ryans said. "Run, pass, it doesn't matter. I want us to move the football and score points."

Houston has mostly done that through the air, with most of its total yardage coming from the passing game. But even with the run game less involved, some trends have emerged.

The Texans' 27-21 overtime loss to the New York Giants on Oct. 25 ended two streaks that had lasted through the first two years of Woody Marks' career.

Houston had been 10-0 when Marks carried the ball at least 11 times in a game since the Texans drafted him in 2025. The team had also been 11-0 when he rushed for at least 44 yards.

Marks rushed 19 times for 66 yards against the Giants, but it wasn't enough to help the Texans win or keep either streak alive.

"He sees the hole and hits it hard," Texans center Evan Brown said. "It's been fun blocking for him. We've got to do a better job giving him a little bit more of a crease to hit sometimes, and we'll keep working at that as we go."

David Montgomery, acquired in an offseason trade with Detroit, got off to a fast start in his first game with the Texans. He scored three touchdowns, and Houston rushed for 124 yards in an overtime loss to Buffalo in Week 1. But the Texans followed with three straight games of 70 yards or fewer. They had just one regular-season game with fewer than 70 rushing yards last season.

The rushing attack has been better over the past three games, especially in the win over the Jacksonville Jaguars, when Marks found success running to the right side of the offensive line.

{ "__type": "devHubFreeformEmbed", "__id": "Datawrapper", "__fallbackImage": "datawrapper.dwcdn.net/oGyBn/mobile.png", "__data": { "datawrapper_id": "oGyBn" } }

Nearly 74% of Marks' rushing yards over the past three games came on runs inside the right side of the line or to the right. The Texans' more experienced starters on that side are right tackle Trent Brown and right guard Ed Ingram.

"I'm not sitting there intentionally trying to run right every single time," second-year offensive coordinator Nick Caley said. "Like, I can promise you that."

Marks' longest run of the season has been 12 yards, though he has had longer runs called back by penalties. A 27-yard run against the Giants was negated by a holding penalty, and his 24-yard touchdown against the Tennessee Titans was nullified by another holding call.

"When you get them big runs and it finally opens up and you turn around and it's a flag, it's just like, dang," Marks said.

It's not just a problem for Marks. The Texans' longest run of the season so far was a 25-yard touchdown by Jawhar Jordan against the Jaguars.

Every team in the league except the Cincinnati Bengals has had at least one run longer than 25 yards. The Bengals and Texans are the only teams with fewer than two runs of 20 or more yards.

#2757. Why Drew Lock is about to take the Seahawks starting QB job from Sam Darnold for good

(Editor's note: Everyone please welcome back Michael Thompson to the Field Gulls staff! He was with us all of last season and is returning for at least the rest of this season)

For the second straight game against the Arizona Cardinals, Sam Darnold will be on the sidelines injured, while backup Drew Lock will be tasked with helping the Seahawks get an important divisional win. After Monday night's debacle, a mauling at the hands (paws?) of the new NFC favorites in Chicago, it seems to be fair to question so much about a team that is less than nine months removed from winning the Super Bowl.

Is Brian Fleury the right guy to be running this offense? Why can't the Seahawks run the football? Why can't anyone get open other than Jaxon Smith-Njigba? How was the defense able to be so easily pushed around by Ben Johnson's Bears? Should the Seahawks make more trades, or are they too far behind Chicago and San Francisco? There's a million questions that need and will be answered over the coming days and weeks, but there's two that I think could potentially answer all of these questions.

After a somewhat of a roller coaster 2025 season in Seattle that saw Darnold lead the league in turnovers, but also orchestrate one of the best offenses in football, Sam had his fairytale ending. A crazy fourth quarter comeback to walk-off the Los Angeles Rams in week 16 helped propel the Seahawks to the division title and top seed. From there you know the story, as Sam played the best football of his life against the 49ers and outdueled MVP Matt Stafford en route to a Super Bowl Championship.

Those are special memories that we will cherish and cherish Sam forever for. We also have to acknowledge that 2026 Sam is not the same quarterback we saw last year. Suffering some type of serious glute injury on the fifth play of the season, there have been moments of brilliance and immense talent from Darnold, but it has been clouded by more turnovers, a complete regression in pocket awareness, and an overall lack of that gunslinger swagger that made Sam so beloved in Minnesota and Seattle. I don't know if it is the injuries, the personnel changes, or not having Klint Kubiak around to be his guide, but this version of Sam is hesitant, and he doesn't believe in himself. I hate to say it, but his level of play looks closer to Jets Sam Darnold than anything he's put on tap the past two seasons.

He's clearly not healthy, but I can't help but wonder if his confidence, in both his offensive line and Brian Fluery, is shot. Whenever this type of situation happens with a QB, John Schneider and Mike Macdonald can do one of two things. They can fire Fluery and try to recreate an environment as close to last year as possible for Sam, or they can have Sam take a seat on the bench.

Benching Sam would have sent shockwaves through the NFL, and would bring all sorts of negative attention and drama to a team that needs to figure itself out as quickly as possible. But if Sam is not 100%, could they try to find themselves more stable footing on offense, while Sam could get right? I think we're seeing a soft benching.

With the Seahawks likely favored over the Cardinals at home and essentially a home game next week at Las Vegas before the bye, this could give Darnold three weeks to get right, physically and mentally, while the Seahawks believe they can stay alive as their playoff hopes feel like they're fading fast.

Drew Lock was put in one of the toughest positions in week one. You're the backup to the defending Super Bowl winning QB, and in the first two minutes, he's hurt and you're going in, against a pissed off New England Patriots team and the entire football world watching.

His first half was ugly, but once he and the team settled in, we saw a version of Lock that we had not seen before. After nearly giving the game away on a duck to Christian Gonzalez, Drew Lock was an efficient game manager, going 16/22 for 187 yards and the massive 4th down touchdown find to JSN. He also had a huge 14-yard scramble on his final drive of the game that should have ended the game if not for penalties.

His pocket awareness and mobility allowed plays to develop a bit more for a rookie offensive coordinator, and the championship defense held firm to be a contender in New England. Against the Cardinals on the road, Lock once again looked comfortable and played his best game ever as a Seahawk.

In the desert, Drew went 19/26 for 235 yards and three touchdowns (all to JSN). It was honestly an Apex Alex Smith performance from Lock, as he achieved his two most basic functions: don't turn the ball over and feed JSN. In what ended up a 31-7 win that was very similar to what the Bears just did to Seattle, Lock could have done even more damage if not for turnovers and drops.

Fair or not, the Seahawks had some of their best running in the small sample size with Lock running the show. Pair an average running game with a QB that was 15/15 under center and 13/13 in play action during his 7+ quarters of play, and you have a team that is going to find a way to take care of the ball and squeeze the life out of their opponents.

Seattle is currently 15th in scoring at 23.1 ppg and 7th in scoring defense at 19.9 ppg. When you look back to last year, the offense is nearly a touchdown worse (28.4) while the defense is giving up almost an extra field goal a game (17.2). They're not as dominant this year, and the turnovers carry more weight than last year. This team can get back into the hunt and hope to make the playoffs, but they cannot be fourth in the league at 14 turnovers and a -1 turnover differential. Sam could not fix this problem, while Drew never showed it was a problem in his small sample size.

With Drew at the helm, the Seahawks were 2-0, and people were talking about the Seahawks as the prohibitive favorite to repeat. Lock had proven the floor was high because our backup could be a very good QB in this current environment, but Sam's ceiling made the decision to go back easy.

Now, the game has changed. As Sam (however you want to divide up the blame pie) and this offense have shit the bed, Drew will be asked once again to come in and help keep the season alive. If Lock plays well, just competent top 13-15 guy level of football, the Seahawks are going to go 2-0.

If the Seahawks get to 4-0 with giving the Rock to Lock, we will have the most fascinating bye week in team history. With a potentially season-defining road contest at San Francisco after the bye, will the team really take the ball out of Drew's hands, if he's undefeated? I have no doubt the team loves Sam, but there's no world in which the locker room will allow a switch once again, especially if the team is undefeated with Lock under center.

It's a big if, IF the Seahawks went into Levi's Stadium again, and came out victorious with Drew Lock, then the job will be his until the Seahawks are eliminated or are playing on Super Bowl Sunday.

And this team still has that potential in them. This is still a championship defense. JSN absolutely has the ability to carry a team on a deep playoff run. They just need a quarterback that can channel the ghosts of Jeff Hostetler, Trent Dilfer, Brad Johnson, and Nick Foles.

It feels crazy that we have gotten to this point with Sam and Drew, but with the ball in Lock's hands, I think there's a real chance he doesn't give it back, and we have seen the last snaps of Sam Darnold at quarterback for the Seattle Seahawks.

#2754. NBA Rookie Rankings: Cameron Boozer, Yaxel Lendeborg lead early list of first-year phenoms

We're only a little over two weeks into the NBA regular season. It may seem a bit early to check in on this year's collection of rookies, but if we are being honest … this group of talent is that good.

To me, the early part of the season is all about curiosity. Teams don't have all of their "go-tos" in place, game plans are not quite as firm, rotations are expanded, and teams are figuring out which combinations and schemes work. Why not apply that to these young players trying to find their way?

What feels unique this year is that there is so much new talent being asked to contribute right away on so many different teams. Taking a glimpse this early in the season allows us to see what is working well and to understand the areas of opportunity. Then we can track where growth takes place, where consistency solidifies, and what happens when some of these scouting reports get updated.

I am always one to gently tap the patience button with young players. A slow start can still bring important reps that aid in development down the line. A quick rise can be met with resistance and stagnation.

The best thing you can do as a rookie is showcase a knack for something you bring to the table every single night. The more you do that, the more opportunity you will have to showcase the other things you can do.

Here are my top 10 rookies early in the season:

If you're wondering why the Grizzlies were the league's last undefeated team and matched their best start in franchise history, you can point to Boozer, who last week became the second-youngest player in NBA history to record a triple-double. The versatility of his game, mixed with what the Grizzlies have wanted to do offensively, has been a hand-in-glove fit.

Boozer can be used at both the 4 and the 5. At the 4, his ability to space and keep things flowing allows Memphis to run actions on both sides of the floor. If teams want to switch, Boozer has no issue going right to the post. His ability to win mismatches has been key: patience on his catch, an effort to get to his spot. If help comes, he can pass it out, which allows Memphis to attack tilted defenses. When moved to the 5, his ability to screen, roll, and quickly get to space opens things up. The short-roll passing speaks for itself, but pay attention to his timing and footwork when he screens.

His ability to mix in catch-and-shoot 3s has helped, too, as some of his finishing skills continue to develop. His drives have been aggressive — he's at his best when he delivers a blow with his shoulder — but he will have to balance that with gathering early and finishing over size and length. If these are the building blocks at the start, Boozer is putting himself in a great spot to be impactful all year long.

Many things have jumped out at me about Lendeborg's start, but it's the trust he's earned from Steve Kerr that stands out. After Sunday's game against the Clippers, Kerr said: "We scored 124 points and Yaxel is the main reason that we were high-powered." Lendeborg is attacking in transition, and he's involved in pick-and-roll as both a ball-handler and a screener. There is a trust in his ability to see the floor, but also to attack matchups. The Warriors are running their ever-present post splits through him for him to score. He's confidently taken the keys and gotten off to the races.

The blend offensively has been impressive. The drives have been there: he's unafraid to deliver physicality and get to his spot, showing patience, shiftiness and good footwork, and doing what it takes to turn the corner. The passing has been underrated: once he draws help, the ball is out on time and on target. The 3s have added to the overall package: he's the first rookie in NBA history to have multiple games with six or more made 3s in his first seven games. And these aren't just the catch-and-shoot variety, these are pull-ups over the defense. There's a confidence that tells me these reps will pay off down the line.

From summer league to the preseason to the regular season, ruthless aggression has been the name of the game for Dybantsa. There is a level of force that he plays with, including the way he drives. He will have to work on the balance between pull-ups and initiating contact on drives, but what we've seen is an ability to find a way to get to his spots. You feel him the most in the open court — it's almost as if he is gliding at times — and the result could be a pull-up, a spin, or a finish at the rim.

Being paired with Trae Young and Anthony Davis is a good launching point for Dybantsa, giving him plenty of runway without having to carry a large amount of playmaking responsibility. There have been flashes of what he can be as a playmaker, reading defenses and nailing skip passes. He can get to those types of plays within the flow of the offense off wide pindowns without having to create every single one. I am intrigued to see how he builds on his defensive potential, too. There's a level of physicality and activity he displays when his man is in off-ball actions. He needs that to translate to consistent screen navigation.

Wilson had at least 15 points, 1 steal and 1 block in his first six games, which is tied for the second-longest streak by a rookie to start a career. He plays with consistent and kinetic energy in transition whether he has the ball or not. That's the area where he's felt the most comfortable attacking for himself and his teammates. The mix of his shots will be key going forward: he's shooting 68.4% from the restricted area, but 33% or below in other shot areas. He's been a very willing 3-point shooter (44 of his 63 3PA have come from above the break), and when it's falling, it's dynamic.

He's at his best defensively when he's able to showcase his athleticism and timing. Running through passing lanes to get a steal. Appearing out of nowhere to get a block near the rim. He has a knack for being in help position off-ball and closing the window on a pass that seemed opened. Different matchups will produce different outcomes, but one thing that has not shifted is his will to compete.

It appears Acuff will be a lightning rod for those who enjoy the sport of discourse. My brain wonders whether that should take away from what he does well. How much do we factor in the context in Sacramento? How important is the production? And how do we track the improvement? One thing is for sure: He is an electric scorer. He's the first rookie since Luka Dončić in 2018-19 to have three straight games of 25 points, 5-plus rebounds and 5-plus assists. He's currently a top-10 scorer in the NBA. He also just so happens to be taking as many shots a night as Luka and Shai, and maybe that's where the eyebrows get raised.

Acuff is a tough shot-maker, which by default also makes him a tough shot-taker. The misses are going to feel loud. But is he taking what the defense gives him, or is he aggressively seeing space as an invitation to take a stepback or attempt to turn the corner? What's the balance between him making quick decisions and waiting to come off a screen? His scoring is drawing attention from defenses. The Pelicans worked to get to the level and put two on the ball (which opened up some passes). The Lakers not only put Matisse Thybulle on him but also gave him the switch-and-double treatment. Getting those types of reps early has value.

Flemings has grown during this early stretch of the season by taking reliable qualities (effort, defense, passing) and building on top of them. He plays with poise, composure, and certainty. He has a feel for the game and an understanding of where the ball needs to go and when. That's a great quality for a young guard, and even better for a young guard who has speed.

It rarely feels like he relies on the turbo button. He works to get in space, and works to engage bigs. He's not afraid to take a pull-up or turn the corner, but he's perfectly fine taking what the defense gives him and making the right play out of it. There have even been moments where he has seen a defensive coverage, let them recover, and then attacked the other way. That does not mean it's automatic every time down the court, but that ability, plus his lack of fear, is a positive sign going forward.

Despite the expectations and the early results in Utah, Peterson is doing a very important thing for a rookie: He's figuring it out. A Jazz offense based on flow, tempo and movement felt like one Peterson would immediately add to. The rhythm has been slightly off to start the season. There can be a bit of a learning curve to find the gaps in which to place your talent.

In spite of that, the best moments from Peterson have come when he's decisive. Win, lose or draw, a quick decision has allowed him to make the right reads and make the right plays. Adjusting to ball pressure and physicality has not changed his ability to read defenses. In fact, he's consistently worked to play at his speed, mixing in bursts but trying to have a constant cadence to his play in pick-and-roll. If and when the full array of shot-making returns to form (the 3 has been there), the overall package may feel even stronger.

Energy and effort can sometimes come across as buzzwords. But if you turn on a Denver Nuggets broadcast, you're going to see Brazile make a play. On either end of the floor. A block at the rim, a lob catch, an attack in transition. He's going to do something. He's brought a consistent level of effort to a Nuggets team that has needed it.

He has a knack for cutting from the corner or flashing around the dunker spot that fits right into what Denver wants to do (especially playing with Nikola Jokić). Defensively, his ability to rotate, close out, contain drives and contest has been a bright spot. To put it simply: he's all over the place (in a good way).

Mara's preseason showed once again that the Thunder would have a quality basketball player ready to contribute to their machine. The injuries that have been thrown at the Thunder mean Mara will have to contribute a little more quickly than expected.

Mara's defense has shown both his potential and where he can contribute right now. Having the ability to protect the rim with size is one thing; doing it in different ways is another. He has showcased the ability to rotate from the elbow or wing and be in position. Knowing how and when to execute different pick-and-roll schemes with the Thunder's defenders is another positive. His passing ability, meanwhile, fits right into a team that was working toward more movement and having multiple actions running on both sides. With his size and touch, rolling is a given, but being able to flash into open areas will help.

The biggest thing that has stood out to me from Brown is his moxie. No matter what the box score or scoreboard says, if you watch him, you cannot tell exactly how things are going. He has good speed and good skill, but the fun is watching when he truly understands how to use that speed: when to change speeds to throw a defender off and find an advantage, and when to attack in transition, off handoffs or in pick-and-roll.

The passing is something I have also enjoyed watching. He just zips the ball where it needs to go. The shot may bring him to the dance, but the ability to dip into making plays is where the balancing act becomes fun — the moments where he's unafraid to explore space in pick-and-roll and see if he can get to the second level of a defense, or get a defense to help. There's also a willingness on the defensive end that I think will serve him in the long run.

#2750. Dale Jr. Says NASCAR Teams Taking Investors ‘Don’t Pull All the Strings Anymore’

Dale Earnhardt Jr. says NASCAR teams bringing in outside investors give up some control, a trend he called "kind of scary."

Earnhardt talked about the push for investors on The Dale Jr. Download this week, after co-host TJ Majors brought it up.

"I mean, there's all these freaking teams talking about wanting investors. That's wild to me," Majors said.

"That's the way this, the sports landscape as a whole, not just racing, is going," Earnhardt said. "It's kind of scary because as soon as you bring in investors, you lose control, a little bit of control."

"Those investors are going to want results. They're going to want control. They're going to want to, you know, know what's going on," he added. "And now this team that you were pulling all the strings on, you don't pull all the strings anymore."

His comments come days after Brad Keselowski reached an agreement with RFK Racing on Oct. 31 to give up his management role. Keselowski tried to buy RFK, but Jack Roush and Fenway Sports Group turned down his offer.

Keselowski is leaving the team after this season and will stay a passive investor for now while he plans to sell his 20% stake. His roles in team governance, competition oversight and the board have ended. He has said the split was not adversarial. Keselowski joined RFK as a driver and co-owner in 2022, alongside Jack Roush and Fenway Sports Group.

Several Cup teams have brought in outside partners in recent years. Legacy Motor Club announced more members of its ownership group this week, and Joe Gibbs Racing and Spire Motorsports also have outside investors.

Part of the reason is value. NASCAR's settlement with 23XI Racing and Front Row Motorsports made charters permanent, which made Cup teams a more secure investment.

Earnhardt knows the ownership side well. He co-owns JR Motorsports with his sister, Kelley Earnhardt Miller, and Rick Hendrick. The team races full time in the O'Reilly Auto Parts Series and has entered the Daytona 500 the last two years. Earnhardt has been open about wanting to run full time in Cup.

Running a Cup team takes millions each year. Sports Business Journal has reported that charter values are expected to reach $50 million to $100 million.

Earnhardt spent 18 seasons racing at NASCAR's top level and now runs a team in motorsports himself, so he has seen both sides of ownership.

His comments came the same week Dodge confirmed its Cup return with Kaulig Racing. Legacy is one example of how outside investment can work. Co-owner Jimmie Johnson has said new investment diluted his original stake, though he still controls the company.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.
